On SANA, reusing an executed prefix preserves markedly more of the scene than regenerating from noise at a similar strength of edit, learned conditions preserve more background than native prompt switching from the same saved state, and the learned program improves generation quality over native SANA. Later branches weaken the edit, which leaves semantic control over individual operations limited. By converting a single-instruction trajectory into a program of addressable operations, Dancing Diffusion lays a foundation for structured intermediate computation in diffusion models.
item.dc:creator: Cui Enhe, Jinyue Yang, Bojian Yin, Guoqi Li

item.title: StochIKM: Automated High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Individual Patient Data from Published Kaplan-Meier Curves
item.description: arXiv:2610.29122v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Individual patient data are the gold standard for secondary analysis of time-to-event evidence, but they are rarely released, and reconstruction from a published Kaplan-Meier figure could help. Existing methods all claim high fidelity, each judged by whichever agreements it happens to achieve, and each returns a single dataset although the map from figure to data is not bijective. We define fidelity explicitly: a dataset is admissible when it reproduces the risk table exactly, follows the digitized curve to within the image resolution, and respects the printed median, interval and event count. We propose StochIKM, a stochastic algorithm that digitizes the figure with a vision-capable language model and uses the high-fidelity definition as constraints, returning an admissible set of individual patient datasets. A solution is guaranteed to exist whenever the figure has been read correctly, so a failure indicts either the published figure or its digitization. In simulation and in 79 arms from published oncology trials, StochIKM reproduces the published risk tables and medians more closely than LLM-improved IPDfromKM, a high-impact alternative.
item.dc:creator: Liangze Ke, Daniel Zelterman, Wei Wei, Guannan Gong

item.title: AgentMonopoly: Behavioral Patterns and Persona Control in LLM Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.29330v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How do LLM agents' strategies differ, and how much can instructions to adopt a persona change their behavior over a game? We study these questions with AgentMonopoly, an environment where agents communicate, buy and trade properties, and make decisions that affect later turns. We compare models from four families, each at two sizes, in games with identical models, different sizes of the same family, or different families. We also assign one agent a persona, a description of how it should behave, intended to change a tendency observed in games without that persona. The tested models differ in how often they trade, waive rent, and manage cash and properties. Larger models do not consistently win more games. Persona instructions change the words agents use and some of their actions, but the changes do not always match the role across all decisions. These results show why persona following should be assessed through actions and outcomes as well as language. As our findings are conditional on the tested checkpoints, prompts, and five seeds per configuration, the open-source nature of AgentMonopoly provides the experimental infrastructure for further extending these comparisons. Our code is available at https://github.com/SuELS-Group/Agent_Monopoly.
item.dc:creator: Changshun Wu, Mengyu Li, Mathis Marsault, Xiaowei Huang, Chih-Hong Cheng

item.title: TraceForge: Distilling with Your Own Thinking
item.description: arXiv:2610.29680v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Using an LLM to generate training data for another is among the most general ways to train one, and it remains common practice. Some frontier teams have closed that route for their own models: what comes back is an answer, or a short summary, without the detailed reasoning trace behind it. That is a little ironic: they were themselves built on distilling human knowledge, and distilling an open-source model is still entirely routine; the restriction applies to their own outputs alone. Recent work recovers the hidden reasoning by replaying encrypted blocks across models. It somehow works, but it breaks the providers' terms of service, so it is not something a product can be built on long-term. We built the alternative. We take the context and the teacher's answer as input, and generate the reasoning trace ourselves, in the style of the student's own model family. Training is two-stage, supervised and then adversarial: a generator learns to regenerate the family's own reasoning traces from their context and answer, and a critic learns how real a reasoning trace looks. Applied to a teacher's answer, the generator writes one in the family's style. An independent judge rates how likely traces are to be genuine on a scale from 0 to 1: ours average 0.68, real traces 0.66, and traces selected by the critic from four candidates 0.82. These are authenticity scores, not correctness rates. We test the idea on five benchmarks with everything else held fixed. On general tasks the five training corpora are about the same; on coding, the generated reasoning beats Fable 5's own thinking content. With the same 5,000 questions and the same teacher answers, HumanEval+ improves by 3.7 points and MBPP+ by 7.1 at the final checkpoint, and the MBPP+ lead holds at every checkpoint. We suspect that reasoning written in the student's family style is easier for it to learn from.
item.dc:creator: Yan Wang

item.title: Evolutionary Deep Nets for Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring
item.description: arXiv:2303.03538v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Compact appliance classifiers can support local electricity-load monitoring where memory and computation are constrained. We evaluate adaptive sparse evolutionary training and warm-start compression using synthetic aggregate windows derived from household appliance recordings. A completed convolutional network study trains 120 models over four targets and three seeds with validation-only model selection. Two analyses examine compression with approximately preserved binary accuracy and joint improvement in positive-class F1 and sparsity. Relative to a newly trained fixed sparse evolutionary baseline, the selected compressed policy changes accuracy from 91.53%, while increasing macro F1 to 92.40%. Stored weights decrease by 17.36% and active first-layer connections by 23.93%. Refinement requires additional training. Three seeds and unverified source-window independence prevent claims of statistical equivalence or unseen-house performance.
item.dc:creator: Jinsong Wang, Kenneth A. Loparo

item.title: Hearing the shape of an arena with spectral swarm robotics
item.description: arXiv:2403.17147v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Swarm robotics relies on robots with minimal sensing and computation that achieve self-organization at the level of the collective to address a variety of tasks. Yet swarm robotics still struggles with global tasks that require understanding the broader spatial context in which robots operate, such as identifying the shape of the arena in which they are embedded. Here, we introduce spectral swarm robotics, a framework in which robots recover global spectral descriptors of the swarm's geometric structure through strictly local interactions. To do so, robots emulate diffusion to locally estimate Laplacian spectral invariants, quantities normally obtained only through centralized computation. These spectral values serve as compact descriptors of the environment. In the present proof of concept, robots estimated the second Laplacian eigenvalue and used it to classify arenas from a predefined set of shapes with distinct spectral signatures. We show that estimating a single eigenvalue is sufficient for one-shot classification among selected confined environments with distinct spectral signatures. We uncovered a scaling law linking swarm size (a global parameter) and interaction radius (a local parameter) that ensures robust estimation. We validated the approach experimentally on two distinct hardware platforms, Kilobots and Pogobots, achieving reliable classification of arena shapes under realistic noise and sparse-connectivity conditions. Last, we discuss how locally recovering Laplacian spectral invariants opens avenues for swarm robotics in settings where producing efficient collective behaviors strongly depends on the global structure of the swarm.
item.dc:creator: Leo Cazenille, Nicolas Lobato-Dauzier, Alessia Loi, Loona Macabre, Mika Ito, Olivier Marchal, Soo-Hyeon Kim, Nathanael Aubert-Kato, Nicolas Bredeche, Anthony J. Genot

item.title: ACTIVA: Amortized Causal Effect Estimation via Variational Autoencoders
item.description: arXiv:2503.01290v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting post-intervention distributions from observational data is central to many scientific and decision-making problems, but remains challenging due to causal ambiguity, restrictive modeling assumptions, and the lack of amortization across tasks. We introduce ACTIVA, a transformer-based conditional variational autoencoder for amortized estimation of full interventional distributions from observational data and intervention queries. ACTIVA learns a conditional latent prior that amortizes causal knowledge across diverse training tasks, so that a new causal model drawn from the training distribution is handled in a single forward pass, without interventional data, a causal graph, or per-task fitting. Beyond the training distribution, only a parametric shift of the simulator is tested. We provide a population-level characterization of ACTIVA's estimand, showing that, under idealized expressivity and infinite samples assumptions, ACTIVA's learning objective targets a simulator-weighted mixture over the interventional distributions of causal models that are observationally compatible with the input. Empirically, on synthetic datasets and biologically realistic gene-expression simulations, ACTIVA substantially outperforms a correlational baseline, reduces spurious non-descendant effects, and achieves competitive performance relative to strong amortized baselines. On a pair of observationally equivalent models sharing a single observational dataset, ACTIVA recovers the predicted mixture, validating the theory in a finite-capacity model. Our results show that ACTIVA is a promising approach for estimating interventional distributions from observational data.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Sauter, Saber Salehkaleybar, Frank van Harmelen, Aske Plaat, Erman Acar

item.title: The Mathematical Theory of Double Descent as Shrinkage, not Overfitting: Matching Bounds for Path-Regularized Multilayer Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2503.02129v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a nonasymptotic generalization theory for multilayer fully connected neural networks trained with path regularization, for general Lipschitz losses and without assuming the loss bounded, the architecture sparse, or any width or depth limit. Approximation error is modelled explicitly, and along the way we settle an open problem of E et al. on approximation rates in generalized Barron spaces. We treat the underparameterized and overparameterized regimes separately, which is what allows the resulting curve to be non-monotone in the width. We then prove lower bounds on the error itself, valid at every target and at every local minimizer, and combine them with the upper bounds into a theorem asserting that the error - not merely our bound on it - descends, rises and descends again as the width grows, with a peak exceeding the final plateau by a factor diverging in the sample size. Having both sides of the bound also identifies what drives the ascent, and it is not overfitting: once the regularization exceeds the dual norm of the noise, which the prescribed schedule does at every width, a slow-rate oracle inequality controls the error with no variance term at all. The rise is instead the shrinkage demanded by the regularization that the underparameterized regime requires, and we show it cannot be removed by any width-independent regularization under which the theory's guarantees hold. This mechanism is a property of the estimator analyzed here; we do not claim it accounts for the double descent reported for unregularized training.
item.dc:creator: Hao Yu

item.title: Does More Compute Make Every Adversarial Attack Transferable?
item.description: arXiv:2504.20310v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transferable attacks, or transferable jailbreaks, are a particularly strong version of adversarial examples that fool all defenders in a class. In this work, we study when more compute enables transferable attacks. We show that, when there is a quadratic gap in computational resources between attacker and defender, every learnable classification task admits either a transferable attack or an adversarial defense. For generative tasks, this dichotomy fails below a quadratic gap, i.e., more compute for the attacker does not lead to a transferable attack. We prove a stronger result that implies this failure: a defense that spends additional computation after it sees the input can be provably strictly stronger than every defense that publishes a fixed model. This result provides formal evidence that increasing inference-time compute can improve robustness, as empirically observed by Zaremba et al. (2025). We assume the existence of an array of cryptographic primitives: identity-based fully homomorphic encryption, publicly verifiable zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge, non-parallelizing languages, and incrementally verifiable computation.
item.dc:creator: Greg Gluch, Shafi Goldwasser, Anastasiia Struss

item.title: How to Backdoor Image Knowledge Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2504.21323v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer behavior from a large teacher model to a smaller student. It is often assumed to be safe when the teacher is clean, because classic backdoor attacks rely on poisoned labels and triggers in supervised training, whereas distillation trains the student to match a teacher's outputs. We show that this assumption can fail when the distillation dataset itself is poisoned. Our attack injects triggered and manipulated images that a clean teacher already predicts as an attacker chosen target label, which causes the student to learn a backdoor even though the teacher remains unaffected. We evaluate this threat across multiple manipulation strategies, including targeted adversarial perturbations and targeted GAN based class transitions, and study how distillation settings influence both accuracy and attack success. We show that the attack remains effective even at a 10% poisoning rates. The results demonstrate that a clean teacher alone is not a sufficient safeguard: poisoned distillation data can produce a strongly backdoored student while maintaining competitive performance on clean images. These findings show that the integrity and provenance of distillation data are part of the security boundary of data intensive KD pipelines, even when the teacher itself is trusted.
item.dc:creator: Qian Ma, Chen Wu, Prasenjit Mitra, Sencun Zhu

item.title: DetoxAI: a Python Toolkit for Debiasing Deep Learning Models in Computer Vision
item.description: arXiv:2505.05492v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While machine learning fairness has made significant progress in recent years, most existing solutions focus on tabular data and are poorly suited for vision-based classification tasks, which rely heavily on deep learning. To bridge this gap, we introduce DetoxAI, an open-source Python library for improving fairness in deep learning vision classifiers through post-hoc debiasing. DetoxAI implements state-of-the-art debiasing algorithms, fairness metrics, and visualization tools. It supports debiasing via interventions in internal representations and includes attribution-based visualization tools and quantitative algorithmic fairness metrics to show how bias is mitigated. This paper presents the motivation, design, and use cases of DetoxAI, demonstrating its tangible value to engineers and researchers.
item.dc:creator: Ignacy St\k{e}pka, Lukasz Sztukiewicz, Micha{\l} Wili\'nski, Jerzy Stefanowski

item.title: MAVOS-DD: Multilingual Audio-Video Open-Set Deepfake Detection Benchmark
item.description: arXiv:2505.11109v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present the first large-scale open-set benchmark for multilingual audio-video deepfake detection. Our dataset comprises nearly 350 hours of real and fake videos across eight languages, with 59% of data being generated. For each language, the fake videos are generated with several distinct audio and video deepfake generation models, selected based on their quality, via visual inspection. We organize the training, validation and test splits such that only a subset of the chosen generative models and languages are available during training, thus creating several challenging open-set evaluation setups. We perform experiments with various pre-trained and fine-tuned deepfake detectors proposed in recent literature. Our results show that state-of-the-art detectors are not currently able to maintain their performance levels when tested in our open-set scenarios. We publicly release our data and code for non-commercial use at https://github.com/CroitoruAlin/MAVOS-DD.
item.dc:creator: Florinel-Alin Croitoru, Vlad Hondru, Marius Popescu, Radu Tudor Ionescu, Fahad Shahbaz Khan, Mubarak Shah

item.title: ShIOEnv: A Command Evaluation Environment for Grammar-Constrained Synthesis and Execution Behavior Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2505.18374v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce ShIOEnv, a Gymnasium-compatible Bash environment for synthesizing execution-annotated shell input traces. Datasets containing such traces are useful for training models to perform execution-free shell simulation, which in turn is useful for deploying honeypots for cyber deception. Existing datasets, such as NL2CMD and other Bash command corpora, do not include complete execution artifacts (stdout, stderr, exit status, and changes to the system's state) associated with a command's execution. ShIOEnv synthesizes shell inputs, executes them in a controlled system context, and records stdout, stderr, exit status, and structured filesystem and environment patches. Unconstrained (random) generation of shell inputs (command and arguments) results in multiple instances of arguments that are mostly redundant or result in execution errors. We introduce grammar-constrained synthesis to generate syntactically valid arguments with high input irreducibility, which we estimate through self-ablative contrasts of execution artifacts. We prepare 1.6M samples using grammar-constrained and unconstrained synthesis and collect their execution artifacts for 86 Linux/Bash utilities. Using this dataset, we train small language models (CodeT5) and evaluate their accuracy in predicting the actual execution behavior of attacker-sourced Bash commands. These models outperform commonly used rule-based simulation (Cowrie) and prompted large language models by up to 14.2 pp in output edit similarity (O-ES). We enhance the NL2CMD dataset by constructing 500K samples executable in a grounded system context along with their complete execution artifacts. We empirically demonstrate that models trained on grammar-constrained samples outperform those trained on NL2CMD samples by 22.5 pp in O-ES. ShIOEnv, command grammars, and 2.1M samples used in our primary evaluations are released for use by other researchers.
item.dc:creator: Jarrod Ragsdale, Rajendra Boppana

item.title: MoVoC: Morphology-Aware Subword Construction for Geez Script Languages Corrected version
item.description: arXiv:2509.08812v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Subword-based tokenization methods often fail to preserve morphological boundaries, a limitation especially pronounced in low-resource, morphologically complex languages such as those written in the Ge'ez script. To address this, we present Morpheme-aware Subword Vocabulary Construction (MoVoC) and train MoVoC-Tok, a tokenizer that integrates supervised morphological analysis into the subword vocabulary. This hybrid segmentation approach combines morpheme-based and Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokens to preserve morphological integrity while maintaining lexical meaning. To tackle resource scarcity, we release morpheme-annotated data for four Ge'ez script languages (169,806 records) and a morpheme-aware vocabulary for two of them. Scoring every comparison on words held out from the morpheme resource that constrains the MoVoC-Tok applied to that language, MoVoC-Tok has the highest MorphScore in three of four languages and the highest morpheme boundary precision in two of four, with its largest and most clearly resolved gains on Tigre, a language it was not trained on and to which it is applied cross-lingually. The machine translation results reported in the published version are withdrawn. Data, tokenizers and evaluation code are publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Hailay Kidu Teklehaymanot, Dren Fazlija, Wolfgang Nejdl

item.title: Interpreting vision transformers via residual replacement model
item.description: arXiv:2509.17401v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How do vision transformers (ViTs) represent and process the world? This paper addresses this long-standing question through the first systematic analysis of 6.6K features across all layers, extracted via sparse autoencoders, and by introducing the residual replacement model, which replaces ViT computations with interpretable features in the residual stream. Our analysis reveals not only a feature evolution from low-level patterns to high-level semantics, but also how ViTs encode curves and spatial positions through specialized feature types. The residual replacement model scalably produces a faithful yet parsimonious circuit for human-scale interpretability by significantly simplifying the original computations. As a result, this framework enables intuitive understanding of ViT mechanisms. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our framework in debiasing spurious correlations.
item.dc:creator: Jinyeong Kim, Junhyeok Kim, Yumin Shim, Joohyeok Kim, Sunyoung Jung, Seong Jae Hwang

item.title: How Well Does Mathematical Reasoning Transfer Across Languages in English-Centric LLMs?
item.description: arXiv:2510.02272v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent advances in Reinforcement Post-Training (RPT) have substantially improved the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), but it remains unclear how well such gains transfer across languages. In this work, we study cross-lingual mathematical reasoning transfer in English-centric LLMs under controlled multilingual evaluation. We first evaluate a range of English-centric reasoning models on multilingual mathematical reasoning benchmarks and find that transfer is highly variable across initial model choice, target language, and training paradigm. Through controlled comparative experiments, we further find that stronger English-centric initialization does not necessarily lead to stronger relative transfer efficiency, even when it yields higher multilingual reasoning accuracy. Finally, we show that the largest improvement comes from moving beyond English-only supervision: adding a single parallel language yields a substantial gain, while further gains from additional languages are smaller but consistent. Overall, our results highlight the need to evaluate multilingual mathematical reasoning directly, using both absolute performance and relative transfer-efficiency metrics.
item.dc:creator: Wen Yang, Junhong Wu, Chong Li, Chengqing Zong, Jiajun Zhang

item.title: FlowCritic: Bridging Value Estimation with Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2510.22686v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable value estimation serves as the cornerstone of reinforcement learning (RL) by evaluating long-term returns and guiding policy improvement, significantly influencing the convergence speed and final performance. Existing works improve the reliability of value function estimation via multi-critic ensembles and distributional RL, yet the former merely combines multi point estimation without capturing distributional information, whereas the latter relies on discretization or quantile regression, limiting the expressiveness of complex value distributions. Inspired by flow matching's success in generative modeling, we propose a generative paradigm for value estimation, named FlowCritic. Departing from conventional regression for deterministic value prediction, FlowCritic leverages flow matching to model value distributions and generate samples for value estimation.
item.dc:creator: Shan Zhong, Shutong Ding, He Diao, Xiangyu Wang, Kah Chan Teh, Bei Peng

item.title: Revisiting GAN with Bayes-Optimal Discrimination
item.description: arXiv:2510.25609v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We approach generative adversarial network (GAN) training from its original real-versus-fake classification viewpoint, replacing the cross-entropy discriminator objective with an upper bound on the Bayes error rate (BER). Using the Bayes optimal learning threshold (BOLT) loss, we formulate an adversarial game in which the discriminator tightens this bound and the generator maximizes it. We characterize the unrestricted optimal discriminator and show that, under balanced class priors, the population game is equivalent to minimizing total variation between the data and generator distributions. Restricting the bounded discriminator to be 1-Lipschitz yields BOLT-GAN. For balanced priors and the full discriminator class, we establish upper and lower bounds relating its population discrepancy to Wasserstein-1 distance on bounded domains. Controlled experiments on four image-generation benchmarks show improved sample quality and coverage over WGAN-GP under matched architectures, optimization settings, and gradient penalties. At a common 20-epoch budget, BOLT-GAN reduces Fr\'echet Inception Distance (FID) from 60.0 to 44.2 on CIFAR-10 and from 102.5 to 28.4 on LSUN Bedroom-64.
item.dc:creator: Mohammadreza Tavasoli Naeini, Ali Bereyhi, Morteza Noshad, Ben Liang, Alfred O. Hero III

item.title: Deep Learning-Enhanced Real-Time Wi-Fi Sensing Through Single Transceiver Pair
item.description: arXiv:2511.02845v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The advancement of next-generation Wi-Fi technology heavily relies on sensing capabilities, which play a pivotal role in enabling sophisticated applications. In response to the growing demand for large-scale deployments, contemporary Wi-Fi sensing systems strive to achieve high-precision perception while maintaining minimal bandwidth consumption and antenna count requirements. Remarkably, various deep learning-driven perception technologies have demonstrated the ability to surpass conventional resolution limits. However, the theoretical underpinnings of this phenomenon have not been thoroughly investigated in existing research. We find that under hardware-constrained conditions, the performance gains of deep learning in Wi-Fi sensing primarily originate from two aspects: prior information and temporal correlation, which act as specific forms of side information that reduce the estimation error bound. We construct a deep learning-based Wi-Fi sensing system using only a single transceiver pair and design experiments to validate these gains. The system achieves an average human pose estimation error of 0.2189 m and an average localization error of 0.6124 m, while operating in real time at 42 fps on commodity hardware.
item.dc:creator: Yuxuan Liu, Chiya Zhang, Yifeng Yuan, Chunlong He, Weizheng Zhang, Gaojie Chen

item.title: FLAWS: A Benchmark for Error Identification and Localization in Scientific Papers
item.description: arXiv:2511.21843v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The identification and localization of errors is a core task in peer review, yet the exponential growth of scientific output has made it increasingly difficult for human reviewers to reliably detect errors given the limited pool of experts. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have sparked interest in their potential to support such evaluation tasks, from academic peer review to automated scientific assessment. However, despite the growing use of LLMs in review systems, their capabilities to pinpoint errors remain underexplored. In this work, we introduce Fault Localization Across Writing in Science (FLAWS), an automated benchmark consisting of 713 paper-error pairs designed to evaluate how effectively LLMs detect errors that undermine key claims in research papers. We construct the benchmark by systematically inserting claim-invalidating errors into peer-reviewed papers using LLMs, paired with an automated evaluation metric that measures whether models can identify and localize these errors. Developing such a benchmark presents unique challenges that we overcome: ensuring that the inserted errors are well-defined, challenging, and relevant to the content of the paper, avoiding artifacts that would make identification trivial, and designing a scalable, automated evaluation metric. On the resulting benchmark, we evaluate five frontier LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeek Reasoner v3.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT 5, and Grok 4. Among these, GPT 5 is the top-performing model, achieving 39.1% identification accuracy when k=10, where k is the number of top-ranked error text candidates generated by the LLM.
item.dc:creator: Sarina Xi, Vishisht Rao, Justin Payan, Nihar B. Shah

item.title: MarkTune: Improving the Quality-Detectability Trade-off in Model-Embedded LLM Watermarking
item.description: arXiv:2512.04044v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language model watermarking schemes fall into two broad categories: inference-time methods, which modify the decoding process at generation time, and model-embedded methods, which encode a secret signal directly into the model weights. Inference-time watermarking methods incur additional inference overhead and are not applicable in the increasingly prevalent open-weight model settings. In contrast, model-embedded watermarks introduce no additional inference latency-generation uses the standard sampling pipeline-and are particularly well-suited to open-weight settings. However, existing model-embedded approaches such as GaussMark face a fundamental quality-detectability trade-off: achieving strong detection power typically requires weight perturbations that noticeably degrade generation quality. Our key insight is that regularizing toward a high-quality reference distribution decouples quality preservation from proximity to the base model, enabling a better quality-detectability trade-off. Building on this insight, we introduce MarkTune, a theoretically grounded on-policy fine-tuning framework that uses the GaussMark detection statistic as a reward while preserving generation quality through cross-entropy on high-quality human text or KL divergence to a stronger oracle model. Empirically, MarkTune substantially improves the quality-detectability frontier of GaussMark, approaching the detectability of strong inference-time schemes while preserving generation quality and downstream task performance. Marktune also remains robust under the evaluated text-editing and open-weight attacks and generalizes across datasets, retaining substantial detection power on corpora unseen during training. Code is available at https://github.com/zhyzmath/MarkTune-LLM-Watermarking.
item.dc:creator: Yizhou Zhao, Zhiwei Steven Wu, Adam Block

item.title: LLM-Auction: Generative Auction towards LLM-Native Advertising
item.description: arXiv:2512.10551v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The commercialization of LLM applications is the next frontier in online advertising, with LLM-native advertising emerging as a promising paradigm by integrating ads into LLM-generated content. However, classic mechanisms are no longer applicable in this setting where the auction object is shifted from discrete ad slots to distributions over LLM outputs, and existing methods are impractical in industrial scenarios due to ignored externalities or high inference costs. To address these issues, we propose LLM-Auction, the first learning-based generative auction mechanism that integrates auction and generation. By formulating the allocation as preference alignment between LLM outputs and a mechanism objective that balances advertisers' value and user experience, we optimize the LLMs to inherently model allocation externalities without extra inference cost. Theoretically, we identify the allocation monotonicity and continuity of the optimal allocation rule of LLM-Auction, and prove that a simple first-price payment rule exhibits favorable incentive properties under this allocation rule. Furthermore, we build an LLM-as-a-judge simulation environment for quantitative evaluation, and experiments demonstrate that LLM-Auction achieves the state-of-the-art allocation efficiency while approximately satisfying key mechanism properties.
item.dc:creator: Chujie Zhao, Qun Hu, Shiping Song, Dagui Chen, Han Zhu, Jian Xu, Bo Zheng

item.title: Calibrated uncertainty quantification for prosumer flexibility aggregation in ancillary service markets
item.description: arXiv:2601.14663v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable forecasting of prosumer flexibility is critical for demand response aggregators in frequency controlled ancillary service markets, where reliability requirements such as the P90 standard are enforced. Limited behavioural data and dependence on exogenous forecasts introduce uncertainty into flexibility estimates, which can cause reserve overestimation and financial penalties. This study systematically evaluates established uncertainty quantification approaches based on Monte Carlo dropout (MCD), conformal prediction (CP), and conformalised quantile regression (CQR) to construct prediction intervals for aggregated prosumer flexibility and support uncertainty-aware bidding. The approaches are evaluated for a behind-the-meter aggregator in the Danish manual frequency restoration reserve capacity market, using a large-scale synthetic dataset generated with an industry-grade home energy management system and publicly available load, solar, price, activation, and device-level data. Multiple multivariate CP strategies are applied to MCD predictions, alongside CQR using a separately trained quantile regression model. Under nominal test conditions, conformal methods substantially improve joint coverage over uncalibrated MCD baselines. More conservative methods satisfy the 90% lower-tail reliability requirement, while CQR and multivariate CP (MCP) yield narrower intervals and higher economic value, retaining approximately 69% and 68% of perfect-information profit, respectively, under the stricter penalty interpretation. A controlled robustness analysis shows that increasing perturbations of load, solar, price, and activation inputs increase overbidding and reduce coverage and economic performance. The results highlight the trade-off between reliability, economic value, and robustness to input uncertainty in aggregator bidding.
item.dc:creator: Yogesh Pipada Sunil Kumar, S. Ali Pourmousavi, Jon A. R. Liisberg, Julian Lemos-Vinasco

item.title: SpatialMem: Metric-Aligned Long-Horizon Video Memory for Language Grounding and QA
item.description: arXiv:2601.14895v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: SpatialMem is a memory-based system which integrates 3D geometry, semantics, and language with one another in one combined, queryable representation. Starting with casually recorded egocentric RGB video, SpatialMem recreates metrically scaled interior scenes, recognizes structural 3D anchors (walls, doors, windows) as the first-layer scaffold, and associates open-vocabulary object nodes with evidence patches, visual embeddings, and two-layer descriptions to 3D coordinates, enabling spatial-relation reasoning, language-directed retrieval, and QA without special sensors. We test at scale on public benchmarks. On VSI-Bench ($288$ videos, $5{,}130$ questions) SpatialMem scores $37.5$ overall with RGB alone, and its margin is precisely where a metric memory should earn it (room size $41.4$ vs.\ $24.4$ with a same-size frame model). On the episodic-memory task of OpenEQA ($953$ questions) the memory serialised to text is lower than the blind control, but as evidence-frame retrieval it recovers frame-level accuracy, matching uniform sampling at an equal eight-frame budget and pulling ahead as the budget tightens, with every answer grounded in linked 3D evidence. On $12$ ScanNet scenes evaluated using instance-level official annotations, the anchor-first hierarchy assigns the retrieved object to the proper structural parent where open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs essentially cannot ($0.24$ compared to $0.01$ with matched input), a capability difference instead of an overall win. The queryable index has a cost of $14$\,KB per scene without the linked evidence frames, and we make available the suites, memories and code.
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Zheng, Yunze Liu, Chi-Hao Wu, Fan Zhang, Hao Zheng, Wenqi Zhou, Walterio W. Mayol-Cuevas, Junxiao Shen

item.title: Exact and Asymptotically Complete Robust Verifications of Neural Networks via Ising Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2603.00408v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present an Ising-compatible framework for formal neural-network robustness verification under bounded input perturbations. For piecewise activations (both continuous piecewise-linear and discrete piecewise-constant), the Exact Logarithmic Piecewise Model (Log-PW) provides an exact, sound, and complete formulation with a state-optimal logarithmic encoding, reducing the binary variables per neuron from linear $O(\kappa)$ to information-theoretically minimal logarithmic complexity $O(\lceil \log_2 \kappa \rceil)$ via logarithmic SOS2 (Log-PWL) and SOS1 (Log-PWC) constraints. For general element-wise activations, the Asymptotic Step-Envelope Model (Step-Env) leverages Log-PWC to construct sound, refinable endpoint enclosures. An exact monotonic reduction based on Jordan decomposition further extends this framework to arbitrary non-monotonic activations. We further develop a hybrid Benders solver with output-sensitive iteration bounds, leveraging a Helly-based conflict compression theory to avoid generic exponential cut explosion. In particular, for shallow networks with fixed input dimension, this establishes an unconditionally polynomial Benders iteration complexity in network size. Interval pruning, certificate transfer for pruned networks, and layerwise classical--Ising partitioning further reduce spin requirements. Experiments demonstrate exact certification fidelity for piecewise-linear networks and near-reference accuracy for non-linear activations under compact spin budgets. On MNIST benchmarks, Log-PW halves binary decision spins over One-Hot formulations, while Helly-based cuts achieve up to a $13.41\times$ speedup and an $87.6\%$ reduction in master queries over standard baselines.
item.dc:creator: Wenxin Li, Wenchao Liu, Anzhe Jiang, Weihao Li, Chuan Wang, Qi Gao, Yin Ma, Hai Wei, Kai Wen

item.title: Near-Optimal Regret for KL-Regularized Multi-Armed Bandits
item.description: arXiv:2603.02155v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent studies have shown that reinforcement learning with KL-regularized objectives can enjoy faster rates of convergence or logarithmic regret, in contrast to the classical $\sqrt{T}$-type regret in the unregularized setting. However, the statistical efficiency of online learning with respect to KL-regularized objectives remains far from completely characterized, even when specialized to multi-armed bandits (MABs). We address this problem for MABs via a sharp analysis of KL-UCB using a novel peeling argument, which yields a $\tilde{O}(\eta K\log^2T)$ upper bound: the first high-probability regret bound with linear dependence on $K$. Here, $T$ is the time horizon, $K$ is the number of arms, $\eta^{-1}$ is the regularization intensity, and $\tilde{O}$ hides all logarithmic factors except those involving $\log T$. The near-tightness of our analysis is certified by the first non-constant lower bound $\Omega(\eta K \log T)$, which follows from subtle hard-instance constructions and a tailored decomposition of the Bayes prior. Moreover, in the low-regularization regime (i.e., large $\eta$), we show that the KL-regularized regret for MABs is $\eta$-independent and scales as $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{KT})$. Overall, our results provide a thorough understanding of KL-regularized MABs across all regimes of $\eta$ and yield nearly optimal bounds in terms of $K$, $\eta$, and $T$.
item.dc:creator: Kaixuan Ji, Qingyue Zhao, Heyang Zhao, Qiwei Di, Quanquan Gu

item.title: Place-it-R1: Unlocking Environment-aware Reasoning Potential of MLLM for Video Object Insertion
item.description: arXiv:2603.06140v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Video object insertion is fundamental to video editing, yet existing diffusion methods often produce visually plausible but physically inconsistent results. We present Place-it-R1, an end-to-end framework for physically plausible video object insertion driven by environment-aware MLLM reasoning. Rather than treating reasoning as a generic text prompt, Place-it-R1 uses the MLLM to analyze the target environment, infer object-scene interactions, and determine where an insertion is physically valid. The resulting reasoning is translated into two complementary forms of guidance for video diffusion: semantic guidance that describes the intended physical interaction and spatial guidance that provides a valid insertion region in each frame. To further align generation with local physical realism, we introduce Spatial Direct Preference Optimization, which leverages an MLLM to rank generated candidates, and introduces a region-aware preference objective that explicitly localizes physical-violation penalties to the inserted-object region. Place-it-R1 further offers flexible and standard modes to trade off environment adaptation and scene preservation. Extensive experiments show that Place-it-R1 produces more physically coherent and visually natural insertions than state-of-the-art methods and achieves competitive results against commercial systems.
item.dc:creator: Bohai Gu, Taiyi Wu, Dazhao Du, Jian Liu, Shuai Yang, Xiaotong Zhao, Alan Zhao, Song Guo

item.title: Optimistic Policy Regularization: Elite-Statistic Reward Shaping
item.description: arXiv:2603.06793v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-policy agents discard trajectories after each update, including rare high-return episodes. We propose Optimistic Policy Regularization (OPR), which turns those episodes into a closed-form reward bonus: we estimate an elite action prior from top-quartile episodes and add a \reviewblue{bounded transform of the log-ratio} of the prior to the policy's action distribution. OPR needs no auxiliary network, value gate, off-policy correction, or adversarial loop. It is a one-line modification of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)'s reward; yet, on 49 Atari games at 10M steps, $5\times$ fewer agent decisions than the 200M-frame baselines, it reaches a 148.4\% median human-normalized score (HNS; 196.9\% interquartile mean): higher scores than published PPO on $36/49$ games ($p{=}0.0014$) and a higher aggregate median than self-imitation learning, which falls well below OPR when frames and backbone are matched. We pair the method with a theory of when it works. The underlying log-ratio has an exact forward-KL interpretation; its pre-advantage placement propagates the signal through Generalized Advantage Estimation; and, under an idealized local update, its first-order effect depends on a prior-advantage alignment whose sign indicates help or harm. Since alignment varies across tasks and runs, we also study an online gating extension. On a ten-game set, it outperforms the backbone by $+17.4$ median HNS on average across seeds. Controlled experiments test temporal propagation and the tradeoffs of state conditioning and gating, supporting OPR as a simple regularizer with an analysis of where to shape.
item.dc:creator: Mai Pham, Vikrant Vaze, Peter Chin

item.title: Markovian Generation Chains in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.11228v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) raises an important question: how do texts evolve when they are repeatedly processed by LLMs? In this paper, we define this iterative inference process as Markovian generation chains, where each step takes a specific prompt template and the previous output as input, without including any prior data. In iterative rephrasing and round-trip translation experiments, the output either converges to a small recurrent set or continues to produce novel sentences within a finite horizon. Through sentence-level Markov chain modeling and analysis of simulated data, we show that iterative process can either increase or reduce the diversity depending on factors such as the temperature parameter and the initial input sentence. These results offer valuable insights into the dynamics of iterative LLM inference and their implications for multi-agent LLM systems.
item.dc:creator: Mingmeng Geng, Amr Mohamed, Guokan Shang, Michalis Vazirgiannis, Thierry Poibeau

item.title: Brittlebench: Quantifying LLM robustness via prompt sensitivity
item.description: arXiv:2603.13285v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing evaluation methods largely rely on clean, static benchmarks, which can overestimate true model performance by failing to capture the noise and variability inherent in real-world user inputs. This is especially true for language models, which can face human-generated text queries containing mistakes, typos, or alternative ways of phrasing the same question. In this work, we introduce a theoretical framework for quantifying model sensitivity to prompt variants, or brittleness, that can enable us to disentangle data-induced difficulty from prompt-related variability. Using this framework, we design a novel evaluation pipeline, Brittlebench, to holistically evaluate the sensitivity of frontier models. We apply semantics-preserving perturbations to a suite of popular benchmarks, and observe model performance to degrade as much as 12%. However, these perturbations do not affect all models equally: even a single perturbation alters the relative ranking of models in 63% of cases, impacting conclusions about comparative model performance. Decomposing the total variance of both state-of-the-art open-weight and commercial models, we find that semantics-preserving input perturbations can account for up to half of the performance variance for a given model. Brittlebench highlights the need for more robust evaluations and models, and allows us to systematically understand model brittleness.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
item.dc:creator: Angelika Romanou, Mark Ibrahim, Candace Ross, Kerem Oktar, Chantal Shaib, Samuel J. Bell, Anaelia Ovalle, Antoine Bosselut, Jesse Dodge, Koustuv Sinha, Adina Williams

item.title: A Sociolinguistic Analysis of Automatic Speech Recognition Bias in Newcastle English
item.description: arXiv:2603.24549v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are widely used in everyday communication, education, healthcare, and industry, yet their performance remains uneven across speakers, particularly when dialectal variation diverges from the mainstream accents represented in training data. This study investigates ASR bias through a sociolinguistic analysis of Newcastle English, a regional variety of North-East England that has been shown to challenge current speech recognition technologies. Using spontaneous speech from the Diachronic Electronic Corpus of Tyneside English (DECTE), we evaluate the output of a state-of-the-art commercial ASR system and conduct a fine-grained analysis of more than 3,000 transcription errors. Errors are classified by linguistic domain and examined in relation to social variables including gender, age, and socioeconomic status. In addition, an acoustic case study of selected vowel features demonstrates how gradient phonetic variation contributes directly to misrecognition. The results show that phonological variation accounts for the majority of errors, with recurrent failures linked to dialect-specific features like vowel quality and glottalisation, as well as local vocabulary and non-standard grammatical forms. Error rates also vary across social groups, with higher error frequencies observed for men and for speakers at the extremes of the age spectrum. These findings indicate that ASR errors are not random but socially patterned and can be explained from a sociolinguistic perspective. Thus, the study demonstrates the importance of incorporating sociolinguistic expertise into the evaluation and development of speech technologies and argues that more equitable ASR systems require explicit attention to dialectal variation and community-based speech data.
item.dc:creator: Dana Serditova, Kevin Tang

item.title: Measuring the Permission Gate: A Stress-Test Evaluation of Claude Code's Auto Mode
item.description: arXiv:2604.04978v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Claude Code's auto mode is the first deployed permission system for AI coding agents, using a two-stage transcript classifier to gate dangerous tool calls. Anthropic reports a 0.4% false positive rate and 17% false negative rate on production traffic. We present the first independent evaluation of this system on deliberately ambiguous authorization scenarios, i.e., tasks where the user's intent is clear but the target scope, blast radius, or risk level is underspecified. Using AmPermBench, a 128-prompt benchmark spanning four DevOps task families and three controlled ambiguity axes, we evaluate 253 state-changing actions at the individual action level against oracle ground truth. Our findings characterize auto mode's scope-escalation coverage under this stress-test workload. The end-to-end false negative rate is 81.0% (95% CI: 73.8%-87.4%), substantially higher than the 17% reported on production traffic, reflecting a fundamentally different workload rather than a contradiction. Notably, 36.8% of all state-changing actions fall outside the classifier's scope via Tier 2 (in-project file edits), contributing to the elevated end-to-end FNR. Even restricting to the 160 actions the classifier actually evaluates (Tier 3), the FNR remains 70.3%, while the FPR rises to 31.9%. The Tier 2 coverage gap is most pronounced on artifact cleanup (92.9% FNR), where agents naturally fall back to editing state files when the expected CLI is unavailable. These results highlight a coverage boundary worth examining: auto mode assumes dangerous actions transit the shell, but agents routinely achieve equivalent effects through file edits that the classifier does not evaluate.
item.dc:creator: Zimo Ji, Zongjie Li, Pingchuan Ma, Wenyuan Jiang, Yudong Gao, Shuai Wang

item.title: AtManRL: Towards Faithful Reasoning via Differentiable Attention Saliency
item.description: arXiv:2604.16158v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to solve complex tasks, yet a reasoning trace may merely accompany the final answer rather than causally contribute to it or faithfully reflect how it was reached. We introduce differentiable attention manipulation to train salient reasoning with reinforcement learning -- method which we call AtManRL. By optimizing an additive attention mask that identifies the CoT tokens needed to recover the model's answer, we derive a saliency reward and combine it with an outcome reward in GRPO with decoupled advantages. Because both saliency and faithfulness depend strongly on trace length, we evaluate against a sweep of length-penalty baselines that traces the trade-off a pure length penalty can reach, rather than against a single baseline. Across three models (Qwen2.5-3B, Granite-3.3-2B, and Phi-4-mini) and four benchmarks (GSM8K, MMLU, ProofWriter, and QuestBench), AtManRL sits above this trade-off curve by 3.9-4.0pp in saliency, measured as answer changes under mistake injection, and by 5.7-7.7pp in faithfulness, measured as hint verbalization under hint injection, while matching the accuracy of baselines of similar length. These results suggest that training explicitly for saliency is a promising route towards chain-of-thought reasoning that is more faithful to the model's actual decision process.
item.dc:creator: Max Henning H\"oth, Kristian Kersting, Bj\"orn Deiseroth, Letitia Parcalabescu

item.title: Graph Memory Transformer (GMT)
item.description: arXiv:2604.23862v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate whether an explicit learned memory graph can replace the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) sublayer in a decoder-only transformer while preserving the surrounding autoregressive architecture. In the proposed graph Memory Transformer (GMT), a memory cell routes token representations over a learned bank of centroids connected by a learned directed transition matrix, while causal self-attention remains unchanged. In the base v7 instantiation, each of 16 transformer blocks contains 128 centroids and a 128 x 128 edge matrix. Each cell uses gravitational source routing and token-conditioned target selection to return a gated displacement from the estimated source memory state toward the target memory state, rather than a retrieved value. The resulting decoder-only language model has 82.2M trainable parameters and no dense FFN sublayers; the evaluated dense GPT-style baseline has 103.0M. It trains stably and exposes centroid usage, transition structure, and source-to-target movement for direct inspection in the forward computation. It trails the larger baseline in validation loss and perplexity (3.5995/36.58 vs. 3.2903/26.85), while showing close zero-shot benchmark behavior under the evaluated setting. These results support the viability and structural interpretability of replacing dense within-token transformation with graph-mediated memory navigation, without claiming state-of-the-art performance. Broader scaling, optimized kernels, and more extensive benchmark evaluation remain for future work.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Zanarini, Niccol\`o Ferrari, Evelina Lamma

item.title: Unifying Goal-Conditioned RL and Unsupervised Skill Learning via Control-Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2605.06145v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unsupervised pretraining has driven empirical advances in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL), but its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In particular, an influential class of methods, mutual information skill learning (MISL), discovers behaviorally diverse skills that can later be used for downstream goal-reaching. However, it remains a theoretical mystery why skills learned through MISL should support goal-reaching. A subtle challenge is that both GCRL and MISL are umbrella terms: Different GCRL tasks use distinct criteria for measuring goal-reaching performance, while different MISL methods optimize distinct notions of behavioral diversity. We address this challenge and unify GCRL and MISL as instances of control maximization. We identify three canonical GCRL formulations and prove that they are fundamentally inequivalent: They can induce incompatible optimal policies even in the same environment. Nevertheless, they all share a common interpretation: A well-performing goal-conditioned policy is one whose future trajectory is highly sensitive to the commanded goal, with the precise notion of sensitivity determined by the GCRL formulation. Noting that MISL objectives can be understood as measures of skill sensitivity akin to goal sensitivity, we show that MISL objectives are bounded by formulation-specific downstream goal sensitivities. These bounds establish a precise correspondence between MISL methods and downstream GCRL tasks: For every GCRL formulation, there exists a matching MISL objective for which more diverse skills afford greater downstream goal sensitivity. Our results thus lay a theoretical foundation for RL pretraining and have important practical implications, such as suggesting which pretraining objectives to use when a user cares about a specific class of downstream tasks.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Modirshanechi, Benjamin Eysenbach, Peter Dayan, Eric Schulz

item.title: Benchmarking Compositional Generalisation for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2605.08988v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials play a fundamental role in computational chemistry and materials science, enabling applications from molecular dynamics simulations to drug design and materials discovery. While recent approaches can estimate inter-atomic forces with high precision, it remains unclear to what extent they can generalise to previously unseen molecules. Do they learn the compositional structure of chemistry, capturing how molecular fragments and their combinations determine properties, or do they primarily learn to interpolate patterns that are specific to the training examples? To address this question, we propose a benchmark consisting of four tasks that require some form of compositional generalisation. In each task, models are tested on molecules that were unseen during training, but the training data is chosen such that generalisation to the test examples should be feasible for models that learn the underlying physical principles. Our empirical analysis shows that the considered tasks are highly challenging for state-of-the-art models, with errors on out-of-distribution examples often an order of magnitude higher than on in-distribution examples, even when using foundation models that have been pre-trained on millions of molecules.
item.dc:creator: Amir Masoud Nourollah, Irtaza Khalid, Stefano Leoni, Steven Schockaert

item.title: Disentangled Sparse Representations for Concept-Separated Diffusion Unlearning
item.description: arXiv:2605.12122v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unlearning specific concepts in text-to-image diffusion models has become increasingly important for preventing undesirable content generation. Among prior approaches, sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based methods have attracted attention due to their ability to suppress target concepts through lightweight manipulation of latent features, without modifying model parameters. However, SAEs trained primarily for sparse reconstruction do not explicitly enforce concept-wise separation, allowing semantically related concepts to share latent features. To address this, we propose SAEParate, which explicitly separates semantically overlapping concepts in the SAE latent space through concept-aware contrastive learning, supported by cross-attention-guided spatial aggregation that emphasizes concept-relevant regions. In addition, we enhance the encoder with a nonlinear transformation to increase its expressive capacity under this separation objective, enabling more concept-discriminative latent representations. Experiments on UnlearnCanvas demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains in joint style-object unlearning, a challenging setting where existing methods suffer from severe interference between target and non-target concepts.
item.dc:creator: Hyeonjin Kim, Hangyeol Jung, Heechan Yun, Sungjun Yun, Dong-Jun Han

item.title: Manifold Sampling via Entropy Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2605.12338v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sampling from constrained distributions has a wide range of applications, including in Bayesian optimization and robotics. Prior work establishes convergence and feasibility guarantees for constrained sampling, but assumes that the feasible set is connected. However, in practice, the feasible set often decomposes into multiple disconnected components, which makes efficient sampling under constraints challenging. In this paper, we propose MAnifold Sampling via Entropy Maximization (MASEM) for uniform sampling on a manifold with an unknown number of disconnected components, implicitly defined by smooth equality and inequality constraints. The presented method uses a resampling scheme to maximize the entropy of the empirical distribution based on k-nearest neighbor density estimation. We show that, in the mean field, MASEM decreases the KL-divergence between the empirical distribution and the maximum-entropy target exponentially in the number of resampling steps. We instantiate MASEM with multiple local samplers and demonstrate its versatility and efficiency on synthetic and robotics-based benchmarks. MASEM enables fast and scalable mixing across a range of constrained sampling problems, improving over alternatives by an order of magnitude in Sinkhorn distance with competitive runtime.
item.dc:creator: Cornelius V. Braun, Tilman Burghoff, Marc Toussaint

item.title: Learning Unbiased Permutations via Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2605.16755v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning permutations is fundamental to sorting, ranking, and matching, but existing differentiable methods based on entropy-regularized Sinkhorn produce a single softened solution and collapse under ambiguity. We present PermFlow, a conditional flow matching framework that operates directly on the affine subspace of matrices with unit row and column sums. A closed-form tangent-space projector preserves these constraints exactly along every trajectory, by construction rather than through iterative correction, and a nearest-target coupling routes distinct noisy initializations toward distinct valid permutations. The result is a model that captures multimodal permutation distributions rather than collapsing them to a single mode. On a range of problems, PermFlow achieves high accuracy on unambiguous inputs and recovers both valid permutations under ambiguity.
item.dc:creator: Yimeng Min, Carla P. Gomes

item.title: Stop Drawing Scientific Claims from LLM Social Simulations Without Robustness Audits
item.description: arXiv:2605.18890v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The scientific claims drawn from LLM social simulations should be no stronger than the robustness audits that support them. Generative agents bring new expressive power to agent-based modeling, enabling simulations of collective social processes like cooperation, polarization, and norm formation. Yet they also introduce complexity through additional architectural choices, such as agent specification, memory representation, interaction protocols, and environment design. Small perturbations that appear minor to researchers can cascade into macro-level outcomes through repeated interaction, creating a "butterfly effect." Consequently, scientific claims drawn from LLM social simulations may reflect implementation artifacts rather than the social mechanisms being modeled. We support this position with two case studies: a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma and a social media echo chamber simulation. Across multiple models, minor perturbations in persona format and game-instruction framing shift cooperation rates by up to 76 percentage points, while network homophily and hub assignment produce significant and consistent shifts in polarization metrics. We also find that sensitivity is unevenly distributed across both architectural choices and model families: the same perturbation that produces the 76 pp shift in one frontier model only shifts another by 1 pp. Robustness is therefore a property that should be measured per claim and per model, not assumed. To address this validation gap, we introduce TRAILS (Taxonomy for Robustness Audits In LLM Simulations), a robustness-audit taxonomy spanning three levels of simulation design: agent (micro-level), interaction (meso-level), and system (macro-level). We call for robustness to become a first-order validation requirement before LLM social simulations are used to explain mechanisms, evaluate interventions, or inform decisions.
item.dc:creator: Jinyi Ye, Lei Cao, Ding Chen, Emilio Ferrara

item.title: FormalASR: End-to-End Spoken Chinese to Formal Text
item.description: arXiv:2605.19266v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems are typically optimized for verbatim transcription, which preserves disfluencies, filler words, and informal spoken structures that are often unsuitable for downstream writing-oriented applications. A common workaround is a two-stage ASR+LLM pipeline for post-editing, but this design increases latency and memory cost and is difficult to deploy on-device. We present FormalASR, two compact end-to-end models with 0.6B and 1.7B parameters that directly transcribe spoken Chinese into formal written text. To enable this setting, we build WenetSpeech-Formal and Speechio-Formal, two large-scale spoken-to-formal datasets constructed by LLM-based rewriting and quality filtering. We then fine-tune Qwen3-ASR at both model scales with supervised fine-tuning. Experiments on WenetSpeech-Formal and Speechio-Formal show that FormalASR achieves up to 37.4% relative CER reduction over verbatim baselines, while also improving ROUGE-L and BERTScore. FormalASR requires no post-processing LLM at deployment time, providing a lightweight, on-device solution for spoken-to-formal transcription.
item.dc:creator: Wanyi Ning, Yinshang Guo, Haitao Qian, Jiyuan Cheng, Wei Zhou, Weiyuan Feng, Yufei Zhang

item.title: When Should LLMs Reason? Adaptive Inference Routing via Entropy Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2605.22873v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve LLM performance, but its benefits vary across tasks, models, and individual queries. On some tasks, CoT provides marginal or negative accuracy gains while substantially increasing token consumption. We investigate whether early decoding dynamics can help identify when explicit reasoning is useful. Our analysis shows that tasks with larger CoT gains tend to exhibit decreasing early-stage entropy, while low-gain tasks more often show oscillatory or increasing trajectories. These patterns motivate an empirical regime interpretation of decoding behavior. We propose \textbf{EDRM} (Entropy Dynamics-based Reasoning Manifold), a lightweight routing framework whose default heuristic requires no router training. EDRM summarizes early entropy trajectories with a compact, interpretable representation and selects among Direct, Standard, and CoT decoding. Across 15 benchmarks and 7 LLMs, its global and instance-level variants offer \textbf{16--55\%} token savings at comparable accuracy. The Full instance-level configuration combines routing with a short Direct fallback branch; our heuristic-router ablation reports up to \textbf{4.9 percentage points} of additional accuracy from oracle answer selection over routing without fallback. These results support selective reasoning based on early decoding signals and demonstrate the potential of entropy-based control for efficient LLM inference.
item.dc:creator: Wei Xia, Haoqing Wang, Zhi-Hong Deng, Yehui Tang

item.title: How Far Will They Go? Red-Teaming Online Influence with Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.22880v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly participate in online discourse, red-teaming their capacity to support political influence campaigns is critical for information integrity. In pursuit of this goal, we focus on locally deployable open-source LLMs under an assumed threat model in which an operator seeks to avoid detection, prioritizes throughput, and selects released LLM checkpoints without modifying their weights. We introduce an empirical red-teaming framework for measuring LLM Overton Windows (OWs), summarizing expression fidelity across sampled political opinions, and for quantifying how simple natural-language jailbreaks change these scores. We evaluate more than 30 LLMs spanning 10 model families and five countries of origin on English-language, US-focused target opinions. We find systematic asymmetries in political expressivity: models typically express sampled left-leaning content with higher fidelity, mean OW scores tend to decrease with model size, and average expression fidelity varies across countries of origin in our sample. Jailbreak potency also varies sharply across model families, motivating a workflow for identifying effective combinations of jailbreak techniques. Our framework supports audits of political steerability and future countermeasure research.
item.dc:creator: Daniel C. Ruiz, Anna Serbina, Ashwin Rao, Emilio Ferrara, Luca Luceri

item.title: Confidence and Calibration of Activation Oracles for Reliable Interpretation of Language Model Internals
item.description: arXiv:2605.26045v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An activation oracle is a language model trained to convert the activations of another model into natural language. However, it is so far unclear to what extent these verbalizations are calibrated. Crucially, the oracle's verbalization come without any measure of confidence. Here, we compare five methods for estimating the confidence of an activation oracle. Our experiments cover four oracles from two model families (Qwen and Gemma, from 8B to 27B parameters), tested on the secret word task, whereby the oracle is supposed to recover a secret word, that has been fine-tuned into a model but does not appear in the model outputs. Our results with $6{,}000$ samples per method/oracle combination show that the best calibration depends on the availability of a hypothesis space or a calibration set: When an assumed auditor can list the possible answers in advance, the oracle should score each candidate answer directly. Scoring the candidates gives a higher accuracy on every oracle and a confidence that separates correct from incorrect answers better than any other method. When the oracle has to write its answer as free text, the agreement over twenty sampled answers gives the best calibrated confidence, which needs only five labeled secret words to be tuned. When a calibration set is available, a rescaled probability of the answer is as good as re-sampling, at the cost of one generation instead of twenty. Asking the oracle to write a number for its confidence, on the other side, gives no useful signal on any oracle. Code and the patched trainer are available at https://github.com/federicotorrielli/probabilistic_activation_oracles.
item.dc:creator: Federico Torrielli, Peter Schneider-Kamp, Lukas Galke Poech

item.title: Semantic Optimal Transport for Sparse Autoencoder Feature Matching and Circuit Compression
item.description: arXiv:2605.28567v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a central tool for interpreting language models. However, two key SAE analyses that remain difficult to scale are (1) matching semantically similar features across multi-layers and (2) compressing large feature circuits into interpretable supernodes. Although these have been treated as separate problems, we show that both are instances of a more fundamental challenge, which we frame as the estimation of semantic distances between SAE features that lie on different activation manifolds. We introduce a distributional framework for this problem, in which each feature is represented not by a single decoder vector like in the literature, but by an activation-weighted distribution over the hidden states that express it. By projecting these distributions into a shared reference space and comparing them with Wasserstein distance, our method provides a unified semantic metric for cross-layer feature comparison. We prove that our representation is invariant to activation rescaling, stable under perturbations, and recovers true matches under finite-sample margin conditions. Empirically, our method outperforms decoder-vector and LLM-based baselines and captures subtle functional distinctions between related features. Notably, our method compresses large feature circuits into interpretable supernodes automatically.
item.dc:creator: Tue M. Cao, Nguyen Do, My T. Thai

item.title: Rethinking Molecular Text Representations for LLMs: An Empirical Study
item.description: arXiv:2606.03057v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for molecular tasks, but it remains unclear which molecular representation to use. We present a systematic benchmark, MolRepBench, to evaluate LLM molecular competence across nine representations and eight chemical tasks. We benchmark 16 LLMs across five model families, including reasoning and non-reasoning variants, chemistry-specialized LLMs, and closed frontier models. Performance is strongly representation-dependent and no single representation wins across tasks, though CML is the best, followed by MolJSON, InChI and canonical SMILES. Explicit structured text representations (CML and MolJSON) dominate structural tasks; IUPAC dominates semantic tasks, winning molecule retrieval for all 16 LLMs; and SMILES variants are rarely optimal despite their prevalence in pretraining. Chemistry-specialized models perform well with SMILES at the cost of large degradations with structured text representations, suggesting SMILES-only evaluation rewards specialization that does not generalize. Using LLM-as-a- judge, we find that IUPAC produces the highest fraction of correct molecule generations. A mechanistic study via tokenization audits, linear probes, and attention shows that representations are encoded differently inside the model; for example, structured representations require more attention across the molecular span. Our results argue against representation-invariant evaluation and motivate task-aware representation routing for LLM-based chemistry.
item.dc:creator: Arun Raja, Garrett M. Morris, Kian Ming A. Chai

item.title: Behavioral Consistency in Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2606.07581v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A trained model is usually described by its weights, as if the weights fixed its behavior. In practice the same weights are run by different programs. Training uses high-precision accumulation and fixed tensor shapes, while serving uses low-precision arithmetic, fused attention kernels, a paged key-value cache, and dynamic batching. These programs produce different next-token distributions from identical weights. We make this dependence explicit by indexing a policy by the kernel that executes it, and we propose kernel contracts, which state how far a serving kernel may drift from a reference kernel on each slice of traffic and what the serving system should do when a limit is exceeded. We prove non-asymptotic bounds that link the logit difference between two kernels to total-variation and KL divergence, to the change in expected reward, to the bias of policy gradients computed from rollouts generated by another kernel, and to whether the greedy token can change. We test the bounds and the contracts in GPU experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Hugging Face and vLLM. The bounds hold on every prompt we measured. Lower precision, a different serving engine, and a different batch size each change the generated token on some prompts, and these changes concentrate on prompts where the model is nearly undecided between two tokens. A kernel can therefore look fine on aggregate metrics while behaving differently on exactly these prompts. Checking a contract separately on each slice of traffic catches these cases.
item.dc:creator: Lan Wu, Bruce Changlong Xu

item.title: Hacking Generative Perplexity: Why Unconditional Text Evaluation Needs New Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2606.08417v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have emerged as the leading non-autoregressive alternative to language modeling. Because their likelihoods are intractable, generative perplexity (gen-PPL) has become the de facto standard for reporting unconditional generation quality. We analyze why gen-PPL is unreliable as a measure of generation quality. Across samples, it is minimized by always emitting the scorer's most likely sequence. Per-sample unigram entropy does not measure this loss of diversity. Within a sample, gen-PPL rewards predictability under the scorer, which need not correspond to text quality. To make this failure explicit, we construct four training-free samplers that reach or beat trained-model gen-PPL on LM1B and OpenWebText at non-degenerate unigram entropy, while producing text that is incoherent by construction. We then rebenchmark recent DLMs using distributional discrepancies and diversity diagnostics, and compare their rankings with LLM judgments. As part of this evaluation, we introduce a compression-based discrepancy that measures local coverage and fidelity, the two directions of the KL divergence between real and generated text. We argue that DLM progress should be evaluated with a set of metrics that expose different properties of generated text.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Franca, Alexander Tong

item.title: Measuring Pretraining Contamination in Public Medical Vision-Language Benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2606.10066v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are evaluated on public benchmarks whose images and question-answer pairs have been freely available for years, yet reported accuracy assumes that these examples were not in the training data. We test this assumption for open VLMs on SLAKE-En, PathVQA, and VQA-RAD, and on a public mirror of OmniMedVQA, using four detectors: image near-neighbour search against PMC-OA-beta, canonical-order exchangeability, cohort-relative Min-K%++ tail enrichment, and cross-model top-K overlap. On the image side, 19.8% of SLAKE-En images have an unusually close neighbour in PMC-OA-beta under SigLIP-B-16 (4.2% under SigLIP-SO400M), while out-of-domain control images produce no flags. Manual inspection shows that these are images of the same modality and view from different patients, not exact copies, so we read the signal as overlap in image sources rather than memorization of individual images. On the text side, Qwen2.5-VL shows an exchangeability signal on SLAKE-En that survives an ordering ablation and two non-medical baseline models, and on the OmniMedVQA mirror exchangeability fires for five medical and general VLMs while BLIP-2 does not. The other two detectors fail a simple control: BLIP-2, which has no plausible exposure to medical VQA data, reproduces their apparent positive signals. Cohort-relative Min-K%++ and top-K overlap are therefore unreliable as standalone contamination signals for small groups of medical VLMs and should be checked against an outside baseline model.
item.dc:creator: Bruce Changlong Xu, Lan Wu, Alexander Ryu

item.title: Beyond Prompt and Parser Engineering: Soft-Prompt Tuning for Automated LLM Evaluation
